newsitem.title: USA: Swiss bank guard challenges UBS document disclosure.
newsitem.headline: Swiss bank guard challenges UBS document disclosure.

text.p: The Swiss watchman who saved Holocaust-era documents from being shredded by Switzerland's biggest bank on Tuesday accused his former employer of failing to disclose the contents of all of the files he rescued.

Christoph Meili, a private security guard who was fired from his job at the Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS), showed reporters a list of what he said were more than 45 Jewish-owned properties from the 1930s to 1945.
After months of refusing to disclose the contents of the documents Meili saved from the bank's shredders, UBS announced on Monday that they concerned 31 properties during that era.

"UBS did not tell the truth about these documents and still is not telling the truth about the documents they destroyed and what I found," Meili told reporters at the offices of his Manhattan attorney Edward Fagan.

Apparently by pre-arrangement, Meili handed the list to an aide to New York Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, the Republican chairman of the Senate Banking Committee and a key figure in forcing Switzerland to open the probe of dormant Holocaust-era bank accounts.

Meili fled to the United States from Switzerland in April, saying he felt his life was in danger. He was being investigated for breaking Switzerland's bank-secrecy laws after handing the documents over to a Jewish group in Zurich.

The 28-year-old security guard charged that UBS had also failed to disclose information from other documents he saved, "showing loans to German companies in World War II or the documents about the German chemical and submarine manufacturing companies, or the ledger sheets of German companies with bank accounts in Swiss banks" in the Second World War.

With his wife Giuseppina Meili at his side on Tuesday, the former watchman said he had received numerous death threats in his home country. He declined to disclose in which city or state he and his family now live.

Moves are being made in Congress to give Meili and his family permanent resident status in the United States. Meili, a father of two young children, said he had job offers but could not accept one until he became a permanent resident.
"Christoph will wait until a bill has passed in Congress that will give him permanent residence and then he will testify whenever Mr. D'Amato holds another hearing," Fagan said.

Fagan is also the attorney for plaintiffs in separate class-action lawsuits filed in New York by Holocaust survivors and heirs who are demanding billions of dollars or records from Swiss banks. The banks include the three biggest: UBS, Credit Suisse Group and Swiss Bank Corp.
A hearing is scheduled for Thursday in Brooklyn Federal Court.
The lawsuits, seeking damages of at least $20 billion, are the key remaining obstacles to Swiss efforts to quell an international controversy over the fate of Holocaust-era assets.

The banks took a big step toward appeasing their main critics, the World Jewish Congress, by breaking secrecy last week to publish over 1,870 names of foreigners who opened Swiss accounts before the end of the Second World War in 1945 and had mostly gone unheard from since then.
Lawyers for the plaintiffs argue that individual victims, not organisations like the World Jewish Congress, should be able to look into records directly from the banks.
